name: hazel tree

attributes.attribute: sacred tree of the Celts believed to bear nuts of wisdom
nut-eating fish, especially salmon, gained wisdom shown by spots on their flesh
grew at the sources of the Boyne and Shannon, shading Connla's Well and the Well of Segais
bards carved staffs from its wood and burning hazel was taboo
twigs guided water-witches and fairies were thought to live in the tree

sources: Hull, Eleanor. Folklore of the British Isles. London: Methuen & Co., Ltd., 1928, 128-129.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The hazel is one of the most revered trees among the Celts. Species of the genus Corylus. The Celts believed it produced nuts of wisdom. Nuts grew when the tree stood at the sources of great rivers. Fish, especially salmon, ate the nuts, and each nut left a spot on the flesh. The most spotted fish carried the most wisdom to whoever ate it. The Boyne and the Shannon both had magical hazel groves at their sources. Uneaten nuts became bubbles of inspiration. The Shannon's source in Co. Cavan bubbles from underground springs that feed the pool. Hazel trees shaded Connla's Well in Co. Tipperary. Anyone who ate their nuts became a brilliant bard and scholar. Koch's encyclopedia confirms this. The Well of Segais, named for the source of the Boyne, held nine hazel trees. Mortals who ate the hazelnuts or the blessed salmon gained the gifts of prophecy and poetry. The connection of the hazelnut with wisdom is deep. Bards carved their staffs from hazel wood. Burning the wood of the hazel was taboo. Hazel twigs still guide water-witches to underground streams. In the Americas the unrelated witch-hazel, genus Hamamelis, has the same reported power. Hazel and thorn are trees that fairies were thought to inhabit. In Ireland people once described Tara as a hazel grove. In Scotland the word Carlton, from the old Celtic Calltuinn, names a place where a sacred hazel grove thrived.
objective: Document the hazel as the Celtic sacred tree of wisdom and prophecy.
key_results: Record the wisdom-nut belief and the speckled salmon.
Describe the sacred groves at the Boyne and Shannon sources.
Note the bard staffs, the burning taboo, and the fairy and water-witch lore.
evidence: Monaghan, P. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore (2008): hazel entry.
Koch, J. The Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia (2006): Well of Segais and the nine hazel trees.
